title: DOM Security and Trusted Values knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the purpose of “DOM Security and Trusted Values”?
options: DOM Security and Trusted Values means the browser can enforce all permissions without the backend.
DOM Security and Trusted Values removes the need for error handling, accessibility checks and tests.
DOM Security and Trusted Values should be implemented by copying a snippet without checking the Angular version.
DOM Security and Trusted Values helps explain and implement one part of an Angular application; choose the API pattern that matches the behavior and verify it.
questions.answer_key: DOM Security and Trusted Values helps explain and implement one part of an Angular application; choose the API pattern that matches the behavior and verify it.
questions.explanation: DOM Security and Trusted Values is a concept in the supplied Angular curriculum. Its correct application depends on the intended behavior, surrounding context and verification.

questions.prompt: How should a learner work with “Security contexts” in this lesson?
options: Assume “Security contexts” works identically across every Angular major and runtime.
Use “Security contexts” to bypass runtime validation of external or user-provided values.
Connect “Security contexts” to the lesson goal, use a focused example, and validate the behavior in the selected Angular environment.
Treat “Security contexts” as a reason to skip the surrounding application context.
questions.answer_key: Connect “Security contexts” to the lesson goal, use a focused example, and validate the behavior in the selected Angular environment.
questions.explanation: The PDF explicitly lists “Security contexts” under DOM Security and Trusted Values. Anchor it in a small example and check the behavior rather than relying on a memorized phrase.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest verification approach for “DOM Security and Trusted Values”?
options: Ignore a failing test if the component looks correct in one browser.
Run the example in a compatible local Angular workspace, test the expected result and one failure case, and document any version limitation.
Assume an SVG diagram proves the code compiled and passed tests.
Treat a successful client-side render as backend authorization evidence.
questions.answer_key: Run the example in a compatible local Angular workspace, test the expected result and one failure case, and document any version limitation.
questions.explanation: Verification evidence should match the running environment. Static teaching snippets are not compiler output, and frontend checks do not replace backend authorization.
